ser.etymology: The DLE traces the modern infinitive to older seer, whose entry gives Latin sedēre, meaning to sit. This is the history of the infinitive; the highly irregular modern conjugation cannot be explained by treating all its forms as regular changes to that one stem.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ser
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: seer

ser.notes: Soy and somos belong to ser even though neither contains the letters ser. Use the conjugation table for the present-day forms.

querer.etymology: Querer continues Latin quaerĕre, which the DLE glosses as seeking or asking. Modern Spanish uses querer both for wanting something and for feeling affection toward a person.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: querer

querer.notes: In the praise of Paquita, quiere a expresses affection. A person can also say quiero un café to express a wish.

estar.etymology: Estar comes from Latin stare, meaning to stand. The modern verb describes a state, location or situation, including the evaluation está mal in this scene.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: estar

estar.notes: Its historical association with standing does not restrict modern estar to physical position.

decir.etymology: Decir descends from Latin dicĕre. Its central use is putting a thought into words, and it also introduces a statement or opinion. The modern verb has several distinct-looking stems, including digo and the subjunctive diga.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decir

decir.notes: Diga here belongs to decir; it follows the speaker’s judgment about saying the boast aloud.

adorar.etymology: The DLE derives adorar from Latin adorāre. Spanish retains a worship sense and also uses the word for very strong affection or liking, which is the sense in Paquita’s boast.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: adorar

llevar.etymology: Llevar continues Latin levāre, meaning to raise. Its modern meanings extend well beyond lifting: they include carrying, directing or handling affairs, and expressing how long something has continued.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: llevar

llevar.notes: The lesson contrasts llevamos más de veinticinco años with llevamos a Macarena García: elapsed time in the first, managing a client in the second.

empezar.etymology: The DLE analyses empezar as a formation from en- and pieza. The resulting verb means to begin or give something a beginning. Its modern stem alternates between forms such as empiezo and empezamos.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: empezar

history.meaning: the components identified by the DLE for empezar

empezar.notes: Empezamos has the same spelling in the present and the preterite. The account of the agency’s beginnings gives it a past meaning here.

ir.etymology: The infinitive ir comes from Latin ire, meaning to go. Modern ir is highly irregular and also works with another verb to express motion, a future action or a gradually developing process.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ir

ir.notes: In hemos ido creciendo, ido is the past participle of ir. The expression describes gradual growth; it does not describe a journey.

crecer.etymology: Crecer continues Latin crescĕre. The Spanish verb covers physical growth as well as increases in the size or activity of things such as a company or business.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crecer

crecer.notes: Creciendo is its gerund. The agency is the thing growing in the scene.

generar.etymology: Generar comes from Latin generāre. The modern verb can refer to bringing something into existence, producing an effect, or procreating; the agency slogan uses it for producing success.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: generar

haber.etymology: Haber descends from Latin habēre, which the DLE glosses as to have. Modern Spanish uses it especially as the helper in compound tenses and in impersonal expressions of existence.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: haber

haber.notes: Ha llamado and hemos ido use haber as an auxiliary. Ordinary possession is normally expressed with tener.

llamar.etymology: Llamar continues Latin clamāre. Its present-day senses still include attracting attention by calling out, and they also include making a telephone call and naming someone.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: llamar

llamar.notes: The scene asks whether Maca has telephoned. The past participle llamado stays unchanged after haber.

actuar.etymology: The DLE traces actuar to Medieval Latin actuare. Spanish uses it for taking action or performing the functions of a role, and for playing a part in theatre, film, radio or television.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: actuar

actuar.notes: Actuar names the activity of acting in the sentence Actuar es un oficio.

tratar.etymology: Tratar comes from Latin tractāre. The Spanish word covers handling or managing something, dealing with people, and discussing a subject. With de and an infinitive it can express an attempt.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tratar

tratar.notes: Tratamos de trabajar means we try to work. The following de is part of that construction.

trabajar.etymology: The DLE traces trabajar to reconstructed Vulgar Latin *tripaliāre, associated with torture, and ultimately to Late Latin tripalium, a three-timber instrument of torture. The asterisk marks an inferred historical form rather than an attested spelling.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: trabajar

trabajar.notes: Modern trabajar covers physical or intellectual activity, paid employment and practising a profession. Those present-day meanings should be learned in their own contexts.

tener.etymology: Tener continues Latin tenēre. Alongside holding or possessing something, modern Spanish uses it in many expressions for a state, age, obligation or settled understanding.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tener

tener.notes: Tener algo claro means to be clear or certain about it. In the lesson, tiene esto muy claro concerns understanding acting as a profession.

representante.etymology: Representante is formed from representar and the ending -nte. The base verb continues Latin repraesentāre, and the ending historically comes from Latin active present participles. A representative is someone who performs the action of representing.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representante
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: representar
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -nte

representante.notes: For a talent agent, the DLE specifies managing artists’ contracts and professional affairs. The person noun can take el or la without changing representante.

crack.etymology: The praise word crack is an English borrowing. The DLE records it as a person who stands out for exceptional ability; this is the entry relevant to Paquita, rather than the separate economic word related to crash.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crack

history.meaning: the source spelling of the Spanish praise word

crack.notes: Both masculine and feminine person uses are recorded. This scene’s source audio is represented by un crack for Paquita; the character’s gender remains female.

mundo.etymology: Mundo continues Latin mundus. The DLE describes the world sense of that Latin word as a semantic calque of Greek kósmos: the meaning was modelled on the Greek expression rather than its sound being borrowed.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mundo

mundo.notes: Todo el mundo uses world collectively for everyone and takes a singular verb.

año.etymology: Año descends from Latin annus. The Latin double n and the Spanish ñ give a useful visible connection between the older and modern forms of the word for a year.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: año

año.notes: Keep ñ in both año and años. The word names a period of twelve months and also occurs in the Spanish way of giving someone’s age.

agencia.etymology: The DLE traces agencia to Medieval Latin agentia, itself based on the Latin neuter plural of agens, meaning one who does. Spanish uses agencia for an agent’s work or office and for a business that manages matters or provides services for others.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agencia

agencia.notes: The source business is an agency representing performers; the noun is feminine.

modelo.etymology: Modelo was borrowed from Italian modello. The DLE takes that word back through reconstructed Vulgar Latin *modellus to Latin modŭlus, associated with measure or a measured rhythm. The asterisk identifies the reconstructed stage.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: modelo

history.meaning: a diminutive formation behind Italian modello

modelo.notes: Spanish uses modelo both for a pattern to copy and for a person who models. A person can be el modelo or la modelo.

experto.etymology: Experto comes from Latin expertus, which the DLE glosses as experienced. Its modern uses connect practical experience with specialised skill or knowledge, and the adjective can also name an expert.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: experto

experto.notes: Experto, experta, expertos and expertas follow the person or group being described.

éxito.etymology: Éxito comes from Latin exĭtus, meaning an exit or departure. The modern Spanish word mainly names a successful result or favourable reception; the DLE also records a less-used sense involving an ending or completion.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: éxito

éxito.notes: Generating éxito means creating success in the agency slogan. The ordinary Spanish word for a physical way out is salida.

oficio.etymology: Oficio continues Latin officium. The Spanish word brings together a regular occupation, a role or responsibility, and the skill gained through practising a craft or profession.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oficio

oficio.notes: Calling acting an oficio presents it as professional work requiring practice.

gente.etymology: Gente descends from Latin gens, gentis. In modern Spanish it is commonly a collective word for people, so it can denote several individuals while remaining grammatically singular.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: gente

gente.notes: La gente trabaja uses a singular verb. The DLE also records plural gentes; that does not make an English plural verb appropriate in every ordinary Spanish use of gente.

hola.etymology: The DLE classifies hola as an expressive formation and compares English hello and German hallo. It does not identify either foreign greeting as the single ancestor, so no definite borrowing chain or older root is asserted here.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hola

hola.notes: Its familiar greeting use is established. The h is not pronounced in ordinary Spanish.

y.etymology: The conjunction y continues Latin et, meaning and. Its current spelling is different from its Latin ancestor; the DLE treats this conjunction separately from the name of the alphabet letter.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: y

y.notes: It joins Paquita’s name and job description in the introduction.

un.etymology: Un is the shortened form associated with uno and una. The DLE derives that family from Latin unus. The numeral for one also supplies the Spanish indefinite article used before a singular count noun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: un
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: uno

un.notes: Un oficio means a profession. The shortened form un normally appears before a masculine singular noun.

todo.etymology: Todo comes from Latin totus, meaning whole or entire. Spanish uses this inherited word both for a complete whole and for all the members of a group.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: todo

todo.notes: In todo el mundo the complete world stands for everyone. Todo follows the singular masculine mundo even though many people are meant.

el.etymology: The definite-article family el, la and lo developed from Latin ille, illa and illud, demonstrative forms meaning that one. The old pointing forms became everyday markers of an identifiable person or thing.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: el

el.notes: El is the article in el mundo. It is written without the accent used by the personal pronoun él.

a.etymology: The preposition a continues Latin ad. It now introduces a destination or limit, an indirect object, and many specific human direct objects, among other uses.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: a

a.notes: The a before Paquita or Macarena marks a human object. The same spelling participates in the expression poco a poco.

muchísimo.etymology: Muchísimo is the intensified form built from mucho with -ísimo. The DLE traces mucho to Latin multus and the superlative ending to Latin -issĭmus; the modern combination expresses a very high amount or degree.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -ísimo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: mucho

muchísimo.notes: Here it modifies the affection expressed by quiere and remains the adverbial muchísimo.

morphemes.meaning: large amount or degree, from mucho

mal.etymology: The adverb mal comes from Latin male. The DLE distinguishes this from the noun mal, which it analyses as a shortened form of malo. The lesson uses the adverbial evaluation está mal.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mal

mal.notes: The evaluation can be translated as wrong or bad in English, depending on the action being judged.

que.etymology: The DLE derives que from Latin quid. Modern que has several grammatical jobs: it can connect a statement to another clause or refer back to a noun in a relative clause.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: que

que.notes: The lesson has que after a judgment and que referring back to gente. Its English translation depends on that role.

yo.etymology: Yo comes through Vulgar Latin eo from Latin ego. The DLE groups it with the related case forms me and mí; modern Spanish uses yo when the speaker is the subject.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yo

yo.notes: Yo can be omitted when the verb already identifies the speaker, or retained for contrast and emphasis.

lo.etymology: The object-pronoun family lo and la continues Latin illum, illam and illud, forms belonging to the demonstrative ille family. The modern unstressed pronoun can point back to a person, thing or idea already under discussion.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lo

lo.notes: In yo lo diga, lo represents the statement Paquita is about to make. This is the object pronoun, not a separate noun with the same spelling.

pero.etymology: The conjunction pero comes from Latin per hoc, meaning because of or through this. Its modern contrastive use introduces a qualification or a different point after the first part of a statement.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pero

pero.notes: The conjunction is a different dictionary entry from the unrelated fruit name pero.

me.etymology: The DLE connects me with Latin me and mihi, including the Vulgar Latin form mi, all belonging to the pronoun ego. Modern me is the unstressed object form used for the speaker.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: me

me.notes: In a mí todo el mundo me adora, the stressed a mí and the unstressed me refer to the same speaker.

más.etymology: Más developed through the older form maes from Latin magis. The modern word expresses a greater quantity or degree and can also intensify a comparison.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: más

más.notes: Más de before a number sets a threshold: más de veinticinco means more than twenty-five.

de.etymology: The preposition de continues Latin de. Its modern meanings include origin, possession, material and subject matter, and it links many words to the complements they require.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: de

de.notes: Agencia de modelos, más de veinticinco and tratar de trabajar show different constructions; one fixed English translation will not fit them all.

veinticinco.etymology: Veinticinco is the fused Spanish number for twenty plus five. Its components belong to the families of veinte, from Latin viginti, and cinco, through Vulgar Latin cinque from Latin quinque.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veinticinco
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: veinte
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cinco
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: cardinales

veinticinco.notes: The number is written as one word. In the lesson it specifies the number of years.

poco.etymology: Poco descends from Latin paucus. It expresses a small number, amount or degree, and the repeated expression poco a poco describes progress in small steps or slowly.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poco

poco.notes: The scene uses the whole expression poco a poco for the agency’s gradual growth.

en.etymology: En continues Latin in. Modern Spanish uses it for location, time and manner, and to introduce a field of work or expertise.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: en

en.notes: In expertos en generar éxito it connects experts with the activity in which they claim expertise.

ahora.etymology: Ahora developed from older agora. The DLE traces agora to the Latin phrase hac hora, meaning at this hour, so a phrase about the current hour became the everyday word for now.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ahora
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: agora

ahora.notes: Ahora mismo emphasises the present moment or current situation.

mismo.etymology: The DLE reconstructs Vulgar Latin *metipsĭmus behind mismo. It combines the emphatic element -met with a superlative of Latin ipse, meaning the same. The asterisk marks the reconstructed form.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mismo

history.meaning: an intensified form related to the same

mismo.notes: Mismo still expresses identity or emphasis. In ahora mismo it reinforces the time expression rather than agreeing with a person.

no.etymology: No continues Latin non. Spanish uses this inherited negative word both to reject a question on its own and to negate a following statement.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: no

no.notes: No, Maca no ha llamado uses it first as an answer and then as the negative marker of the sentence.

con.etymology: Con comes from Latin cum. Its modern range includes company, means, manner and circumstances, so the same preposition can link an action to either a person or an instrument.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: con

con.notes: Con gente introduces the people the agency tries to work with.

como.etymology: The comparative and linking word como comes from Latin quomŏdo. It connects ways of doing something, comparisons and roles; the DLE treats this separately from the obsolete noun como of Greek origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: como

como.notes: Empezamos como agencia de modelos uses it to introduce the original role of the business. There is no written accent in this use.

esto.etymology: Esto is the neuter form in the este family. The DLE traces that family to the Latin demonstrative iste, -a, -ud. Modern esto can refer to a thing, situation or idea just mentioned, without accompanying a masculine or feminine noun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: esto
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: este

esto.notes: In this scene it refers back to the idea that acting is a profession. Its history belongs to the iste family, whereas eso and mismo have a different Latin connection.

muy.etymology: Muy is a shortened form of older muito, which continues Latin multum. The DLE also identifies it as a reduced form of mucho; this older family therefore supplies both very and much in modern Spanish.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: muy
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho

muy.notes: In muy claro it raises the degree of clear. It does not change for the number or gender of the people involved.

claro.etymology: Claro continues Latin clarus. Spanish uses the word for things with light or brightness and also for what is understandable, evident or certain.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: claro

claro.notes: The DLE lists tener claro algo for being certain about it or having no doubts; that is the phrase used in the lesson.

hasta.etymology: Hasta comes through Hispanic Arabic ḥattá from Classical Arabic ḥattà. The DLE also records influence from the Latin expression ad ista, meaning up to that. Its main modern use marks an endpoint in space, time or quantity.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: hasta

hasta.notes: Hasta pronto is a farewell looking ahead to a future meeting.

pronto.etymology: Pronto continues Latin promptus. The Spanish word can refer to readiness or speed and also functions as an adverb for an early or near-future time.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pronto

pronto.notes: Hasta pronto means see you soon; pronto does not describe the person’s character in this farewell.

mí.etymology: Mí continues Latin mihi, the dative form of ego. In modern Spanish it is the stressed form used after a preposition, whereas me is the unstressed object form.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mí
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: me

mí.notes: The written accent distinguishes the pronoun mí from possessive mi. A mí adds emphasis to the speaker in the boast.

paquita.etymology: Paquita is a Spanish affectionate form of Francisca. The relationship is explicitly documented in Báez Pinal’s study of familiar names in Mexico City. This establishes the name form without inferring a longer legal name for the fictional character.

history.meaning: an affectionate or familiar name form

paquita.notes: The character’s established screen name is Paquita Salas.

sources.title: Gloria Estela Báez Pinal, Vitalidad y tradición de hipocorísticos empleados en la Ciudad de México: 1955–1999, p.251 (UNAM)
Netflix: official Paquita Salas cast announcement

salas.etymology: Salas is a place-name-derived surname. The Diccionario de apellidos españoles by Roberto Faure and colleagues, quoted in Villena’s municipal genealogy collection, relates Sala and Salas to several Spanish places bearing those names.

history.meaning: a surname derived from a place name

salas.notes: Several places can supply the surname, including Salas in Asturias and places of the same name elsewhere. This does not identify an ancestral location or family history for Paquita Salas.

sources.title: Villena municipal genealogy collection: Sala–Salas, citing Faure et al., Diccionario de apellidos españoles (2001)

magüi.etymology: The specific origin of this character’s spelling Magüi is not established by the checked sources. Báez Pinal records Magui, without the dieresis, as a familiar form of Margarita in a Mexico City survey. That differently spelled example does not prove that this character is named Margarita or that both forms have the same pronunciation.
magüi.notes: Netflix confirms Magüi as the character name. Preserve that spelling; the survey’s differently spelled Magui is comparative evidence, not a verified full name or pronunciation guide for this character.

sources.title: Gloria Estela Báez Pinal, Vitalidad y tradición de hipocorísticos empleados en la Ciudad de México: 1955–1999, p.251 (UNAM)
Netflix: official Paquita Salas cast announcement

macarena.etymology: Macarena is also the name of a Seville neighbourhood and the Marian invocation venerated there. Seville’s official tourism site offers two possible sources for the place name: Bab-al-Makrin, associated with the old northern gate, or Macarius-Ena, described as a Roman landowner. The site presents these as alternatives, so the ultimate place-name etymology remains uncertain here.
macarena.notes: This cultural history is not proof of the actress’s family naming decision and does not supply a settled literal translation for her given name.

sources.title: Seville official tourism office: Barrio de la Macarena
Netflix: Paquita Salas, episode1 and the client Macarena García

garcía.etymology: Auñamendi classifies García as a patronymic surname derived from the older personal name García or Garzia. An official Euskaltzaindia publication also connects the name Gartzia with medieval Garçea. These sources support the name’s historical family, but no certain deeper lexical meaning is assigned here.

history.meaning: a personal name cited in the history of Gartzia
a surname formed from an older personal name

garcía.notes: The patronymic classification is documented; the ultimate meaning of the older name remains uncertain. No particular ancestry is inferred for Macarena García.

sources.title: Auñamendi Eusko Entziklopedia: GARCÍA
Euskaltzaindia official publication, p.118: Gartzia and medieval Garçea

maca.etymology: In this scene, Maca is used as the short name for the client Macarena García, introduced just before the question about her call. This is a scene-specific example of shortening a personal name, the process described by FundéuRAE as acortamiento.
maca.notes: The identification comes from the source scene’s name sequence, particularly native cues20 and22–23. It is not a claim that every person called Maca has the same full name.

sources.title: FundéuRAE: diminutivo e hipocorístico no son sinónimos
Netflix: Paquita Salas, episode1 and the client Macarena García
